title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
hook: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner becomes governor

segments.voice: Yesterday, prison: a false charge, a cell, and a butler who forgot. Your line was the lord was with joseph.

Two years later, Pharaoh has a nightmare. By the Nile, seven sleek, fat cows come up out of the river. Then seven thin ones, all bone, eat the fat ones and look no better afterward. He wakes, sleeps, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. Every wise man in Egypt is summoned. Nobody can explain it. Then the butler, the one who forgot, suddenly remembers a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams. Joseph is pulled out of the dungeon, shaved, given clean clothes, and stood before the king.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Pharaoh says he hears Joseph can read dreams. Joseph's first words turn that around: it isn't in him; God will give Pharaoh his answer. Then the meaning. Seven years of plenty are coming to Egypt, and after them seven years of famine so heavy the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, Joseph says, because the thing is settled. Then, unasked, he doesn't stop at the warning; he gives a plan. Find a wise man. Set overseers over the land. Store a fifth of the harvest in the cities in each good year, so that when the lean years come, the country doesn't die. Pharaoh asks his court, in effect, where would we find another man with the spirit of God in him? He puts his ring on Joseph's hand, dresses him in fine linen, hangs a gold chain around his neck, and makes him governor of all Egypt. Joseph is thirty. He was seventeen when his brothers sold him. Then it plays out exactly: seven fat years, grain piled up like the sand of the sea, then famine in every land. The people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and he answers in three words: "Go to Joseph." Catholics have borrowed that line for a different Joseph. Saint Joseph, the husband of Mary, also listened to dreams and also took his family down to Egypt, and in 1870 Pope Pius the Ninth named him patron of the whole Church. In Latin, Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him.
screen: `NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.` · `SEVEN YEARS FULL, SEVEN YEARS LEAN.` · `STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.` · `GO TO JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: If your season is a full one, think what you could store from it: a little money, a meal in the freezer, a thank-you note to reread on a hard day, a friendship tended early. If it's already lean, notice what a full one left you. If you pray, offer the full years and the lean ones to God; if you don't, just sit with the thought of both.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin ones: a warning of plenty, then famine, that Joseph reads and turns into a plan. Today's word.
Your line: plan for the lean years. A dream read rightly became bread for a hungry land. Day three hundred sixty-three, in the books.

screen: `DAY 363 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BROTHERS COME FOR GRAIN.`

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph as patron of the universal Church, of workers and of families, and the old phrase Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him, especially in March, the month traditionally given to Saint Joseph.

chat.says: What did Joseph actually do with Pharaoh's dreams?
options: Said the answer was God's, read plenty then famine, and gave a plan to store grain.
He warned of a famine, then left all the planning to Pharaoh's wise men.
He read them as a sign that Egypt would win a war within seven years.
chat.meaning: Joseph said the answer was God's, read seven years of plenty then famine, and didn't stop at the warning: store a fifth in the good years.

notes: Joseph's age: seventeen at Genesis 37:2, thirty at 41:46. Confirm.
Pharaoh's words at 41:38 paraphrased ('another man with the spirit of God in him').
Genesis 41:45: Zaphenath-paneah (Hebrew); the Vulgate gives 'Salvatorem mundi' and the Douay-Rheims 'The saviour of the world'. Confirm the DR wording before the trapdoor goes out.
Pius IX declared Saint Joseph patron of the universal Church on December 8, 1870 (decree Quemadmodum Deus). Confirm.
'Ite ad Ioseph' applied to Saint Joseph in devotion and on altars: stated generally; confirm it is fair.
Pharaoh from Egyptian per-aa, 'great house': standard etymology; confirm.
Some readers also hear an echo of Mary at Cana (John 2:5) in the full verse ('do all that he shall say to you'); left out to keep one idea.
